In this case, the patient had multiple bilateral renal stones and a right distal ureteral stone associated with hydronephrosis. Given the stone burden and location, ESWL was selected as the initial treatment modality. This aligns with current pediatric urolithiasis treatment guidelines, which recommend ESWL as a safe and effective option for renal and upper ureteral stones in children. Combined with laboratory findings of high PTH and hypercalcemia, the successful retrieval and analysis of stone fragments following ESWL facilitated the diagnosis of pHPT as the underlying metabolic etiology. This highlights the importance of not only treating the stones but also addressing the underlying etiology to prevent recurrence.

summary.text: A 13-year-old boy with chronic rhinitis, a deviated septum and respiratory infection admissions at age 3 had occult blood detected during student screening in August 2024, without seeking subsequent care. Periumbilical abdominal pain began 1 day before his September 2, 2024 ER visit. He had diffuse tenderness but no fever, diarrhea, other gastrointestinal complaints or costovertebral angle tenderness. Radiograph and noncontrast CT showed bilateral calyceal stones and a right distal ureteral stone measuring 0.5×0.8 cm with hydronephrosis. Pre-ESWL 24-hour urine calcium was normal at 77.76 mg/day; citrate was low at 109 mg/day.

ESWL preceded wet chemical analysis of retrieved stone fragments, showing a mixed stone chiefly composed of calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. Three-week follow-up calcium 13 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 2,232 IU/L and iPTH 296.2 pg/mL were high; 25-hydroxy vitamin D 13.5 ng/mL was low. Sestamibi identified a parathyroid mass anterior to the right thyroid, supporting the source diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism. MEN1 gene testing found no mutations. He transferred for surgical treatment and received an interim calcium-sensing receptor agonist, with cinacalcet mentioned as an example rather than a definite ingredient, before successful parathyroidectomy and postoperative calcium/iPTH normalization. Exact postoperative values, histology and long-term outcome were unstated.

article_limitations: One original pediatric index patient; introductory/cohort cases and generic medication/genetic syndromes remain background.

All 16 original source units and retained text read. No categorical renal dysfunction exclusion, adenoma/cancer, family history, unstated specimen/assay, drug route/dose, long-term cure or complete stone clearance inferred.

Source-reported stone dimensions retain first/second dimension order, without invented axes. Serial sestamibi phases and three-week follow-up retain raw relative clocks; exact time-zero is unspecified. Initial and follow-up calcium values are separate.

Cinacalcet is an example in administered-class wording; exact bridge ingredient is uncertain. Normal 24-hour urine calcium does not support a hypercalciuria diagnosis. Caption-grounded clinical figures and separately inspected pixels remain distinct evidence layers.
